summary.text: Geographical zones divide Earth by latitude into five belts: the Torrid Zone around the equator, a temperate zone on each side of it, and a frigid zone around each pole.
The belts differ in how high the Sun climbs: it passes straight overhead only in the tropics, never in the temperate zones, and its rays always slant in the frigid zones.
The idea began with the ancient Greeks Parmenides and Aristotle, while today's most used climate map, the Köppen classification, groups regions by rainfall and temperature.

facts.label: Torrid Zone edges
facts.value: Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, 23°26′08.9″ N and S

items.prompt: You live on the equator. How often in a year does the Sun pass directly overhead?
items.explain: Inside the tropics proper the Sun passes overhead twice a year; only on the tropic lines themselves does it happen just once.

items.prompt: You live in one of the two mild belts between the tropics and the polar circles. Will the noon Sun ever stand straight above your head?

options.label: No, not on any day of the year

items.explain: In the temperate zones the Sun is never directly overhead; that only happens between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn.

items.prompt: You spend a full year camped exactly at the North Pole. How are light and dark shared out?

options.label: Twelve hours of each, every day
About six months of each in turn

items.explain: At the pole the day is a year long, with six months of daylight and six months of night.

items.prompt: Earth is cut into five belts by latitude. Which single belt covers the largest share of the surface?
items.explain: The Torrid Zone covers 39.78% of the surface, against 25.99% for each temperate zone and 4.12% for each frigid zone.

items.prompt: Why do the polar regions get so little warmth from the Sun, even during their long summer days?

options.label: Its rays arrive slanting, spreading the heat
They are much farther away from the Sun
Their thick clouds block nearly all sunlight
The Sun is dimmer during the polar summer

items.explain: In the frigid zones the Sun's rays always come in at a slant, so they deliver less heat to each patch of ground.

items.prompt: Aristotle thought only the northern temperate belt could be lived in, with the equator too hot and the far north frozen. What turned out to be true?

options.label: Only the temperate belts hold towns
Nobody has ever lived near the equator
People live in nearly every climate
The far north was once warm and is now empty

items.explain: Humans have lived in almost all of Earth's climates, including inside the Arctic Circle.
